title: Tech rebound lifts futures ahead of Black Friday half-day
dek: U.S. stock futures are sharply higher as Nvidia and other AI names bounce after Wednesday's whipsaw, with Asia and Europe also up. Treasury yields are rising as the bond market reopens, and a December Fed hike remains almost fully priced in.
quick: U.S. stocks trade a shortened session today, closing at 1 p.m. ET; the bond market closes at 2 p.m. ET.
S&P 500 futures are up about 1.7% and Nasdaq 100 futures roughly 2% to 2.5%, led by a rebound in AI and chip stocks.
Nvidia is up about 4% before the bell, even as reports say it paused AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries under a new U.S. license rule.
Treasury yields are up 5 to 6 basis points from Wednesday; the 10-year is near 4.91% and fed funds futures price a December hike at roughly 94% to 99%.
South Korea's Kospi jumped 4.3% and Japan's Nikkei 2.1%; European stocks are up close to 1%.
Gold is up about 2.7% from Wednesday's settlement, rebounding from a 14-month low, while Brent crude holds near $96.60 ahead of Sunday's OPEC+ meeting.

blocks.head: AI and chip stocks lead a broad futures rally
blocks.what: Stock index futures rose sharply overnight and held their gains this morning. S&P 500 futures were up about 1.7% and Nasdaq 100 futures up roughly 2% to 2.5%, depending on the snapshot, per Yahoo Finance, TipRanks and the app's market feed. Dow futures were up about 1%. The bounce follows Wednesday's session, when the Nasdaq fell as much as about 4.5% intraday before closing down 0.6%, and the S&P 500 ended down 0.25%.
blocks.why: Technology and semiconductor shares, which led the November selloff, are leading the rebound, so the Nasdaq and the S&P 500's tech sector stand to gain most if futures hold. Holiday volume is light, which can exaggerate moves in both directions.
blocks.watch: Whether gains hold into the 1 p.m. close, and whether month-end trading on Monday adds to or erases them.

blocks.head: Nvidia rises premarket despite a reported Southeast Asia shipment pause
blocks.what: Nvidia shares were up about 4% in premarket trading, around $155 to $156, according to several market reports, after closing down 3.9% on Wednesday near $149. Separately, the Financial Times reported Thursday, and other outlets including the New York Times followed, that Nvidia told server partners not to ship AI servers to buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. The pause follows a Commerce Department rule, effective November 19, that requires export licenses for advanced chips sent to those four countries and Brazil, aimed at stopping Chinese firms from reaching restricted chips through third-country data centers. Nvidia has not publicly commented, and it is unclear how long the pause lasts.
blocks.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in the S&P 500, so its swings move the whole index. The shipment pause raises questions about near-term sales in a fast-growing data-center region and could also weigh on server makers such as Dell and Supermicro, which reports say have told buyers their orders are on hold. S&P Global's decision earlier this week to put Nvidia's AA credit rating on watch for a downgrade, citing governance and key-person risk after Jensen Huang's return as CEO, remains in the background.
blocks.watch: Any Nvidia statement on the pause, and whether license approvals come quickly for the affected countries.

blocks.head: Bond yields rise as the Treasury market reopens
blocks.what: Treasuries were closed Thursday and are trading again today. The 2-year yield is near 4.69%, the 10-year near 4.91% and the 30-year near 5.29%, each up about 5 to 6 basis points from Wednesday, per CNBC data and a Reuters market report. Yields had dipped Wednesday as investors sought safety during the stock rout, despite hotter-than-expected October inflation data.
blocks.why: Higher yields lift borrowing costs for mortgages and companies and tend to pressure richly valued growth stocks and real estate shares. They also support the dollar. With stocks rebounding, some of the safe-haven buying from Wednesday is unwinding.
blocks.watch: The bond market closes early at 2 p.m. ET today.

blocks.head: A December Fed hike remains close to fully priced in
blocks.what: Fed funds futures imply roughly a 94% to 99% chance of a quarter-point rate increase at the December 8 to 9 meeting, according to CME FedWatch figures cited in several reports. That would lift the target range from 3.75%-4.00% to 4.00%-4.25%. Bets on a larger half-point move have faded, reports say. The Fed's pre-meeting quiet period, when officials stop speaking publicly on policy, begins Saturday.
blocks.why: An expected hike is largely reflected in short-term yields already, so the market's focus is shifting to how many more hikes follow. Next Friday's November jobs report is the last major labor reading before the meeting and could move those expectations.
blocks.watch: The jobs report on Friday, December 4.

blocks.head: Black Friday kicks off the holiday shopping test
blocks.what: Adobe projects U.S. online sales of $12.9 billion today, up 9.2% from last year, and $15.1 billion on Cyber Monday. It expects $47.5 billion online across the five days from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, up 7.4%. Adobe counted $82.5 billion in online spending from November 1 through 22, up 9.1%. The National Retail Federation has forecast November and December sales up 4.2% to about $1.01 trillion, but it also said fewer people plan to shop over the holiday weekend as households watch budgets.
blocks.why: Early sales readings can move retail and e-commerce stocks, including Amazon, Walmart, Target and Best Buy, and shape views on consumer spending at a time of rising interest rates. Strong online growth alongside cautious in-store traffic would favor large online sellers over traditional stores.
blocks.watch: Adobe's and Salesforce's weekend sales tallies, likely out Saturday and Monday.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian markets closed strongly higher as the AI selloff eased. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 2.1% to 58,711, per Investing.com, extending Thursday's bounce. South Korea's Kospi jumped 4.3% to 4,915.68, and the smaller Kosdaq surged about 8%. Samsung Electronics gained about 4.6% and SK Hynix about 5.4%, and foreign investors were net buyers of more than 1 trillion won of Korean shares, per Korean market reports. Reports tied part of the Korean rally to hopes that authorities would expand a market stabilization fund. Hong Kong and mainland China also rose; reports linked late gains to Beijing pledging market support, though closing tallies vary by source.

In Japan, Tokyo's core consumer prices rose 2.9% from a year earlier in November, up from 2.6% in October and the fastest in 16 months, though slightly below the 3.0% economists expected, per Reuters-based reports. Short-term Japanese government bond yields rose as the data added to expectations of a Bank of Japan rate hike in December, the Wall Street Journal reported, and BOJ board member Tamura called for further rate increases, according to Saxo.
Europe

European stocks are higher at midday. The Stoxx 600 was up about 1%, Germany's DAX roughly 0.7% to 0.8%, Britain's FTSE 100 about 0.6% to 0.7% and France's CAC 40 slightly higher, per Alliance News and CNBC data. Chip and mining stocks led, and the stronger gold price lifted precious-metals miners in London. The FTSE 100 is on track for its biggest weekly gain in about eight months, Alliance News reported. Traders have also cited the U.S. tariff proposals announced Wednesday, which were seen as milder than feared.
Currencies

The dollar is steady in thin trading. The dollar index is near 103.8, just below its highest level since March 2025, and is on track for a third straight monthly gain, per Reuters. Expectations for further Fed hikes are the main support. The euro is around $1.097 to $1.098, little changed. The yen is near 159.2 per dollar, close to levels where Japanese officials have voiced concern in the past; the Tokyo inflation data and BOJ hike talk have not lifted it so far. The pound is near $1.311, and China's yuan is around 6.66 per dollar.

U.S. futures point to a strong open after Wednesday's partial recovery. Nasdaq 100 futures are leading, up roughly 2% or more, with S&P 500 futures up about 1.7% and Dow futures around 1%. The gains reflect a rebound in chip and AI stocks, which have been hit hardest this month, and follow strength in Asia and Europe. Smaller companies outperformed on Wednesday, with the Russell 2000 up 0.7%, and the question today is whether money rotates back into big tech.

Keep the context in mind: today's session ends at 1 p.m. ET, and post-Thanksgiving volume is typically among the lightest of the year, so price moves can be larger than usual and may not carry into next week. Volatility has been elevated through November, and the Nasdaq 100 remains on course for a weak month despite this week's rebound.

Treasury yields are moving higher as cash bonds trade for the first time since Wednesday. The 2-year yield is near 4.69%, the 10-year near 4.91% and the 30-year near 5.29%, each up roughly 5 to 6 basis points. The gap between the 2-year and 10-year is about 23 basis points, and the 30-year sits about 38 basis points above the 10-year, a moderately upward-sloping curve. The 10-year traded above 5% in mid-November, so yields remain below this month's highs.

The Fed's target range is 3.75% to 4.00%. Fed funds futures price a quarter-point hike on December 9 at roughly 94% to 99%, per CME FedWatch figures cited by several outlets, after October's PCE report showed inflation at 3.8% overall and 3.3% for the core measure. Governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month that a half-point move may be needed, but reports say bets on a larger hike have faded. Some analysts say markets are also pricing another hike in January. The Beige Book, released Wednesday, showed growth slowing slightly in some regions and wage pressures picking up for hard-to-fill jobs.
Fed speakers today

items: No Fed officials were found on today's public schedule.
The pre-meeting blackout runs from Saturday, November 28, through December 10, per the Atlanta Fed, so no policy comments are expected until after the December 9 decision.

blocks.text: In Wednesday's session, the most recent full day, materials led the S&P 500 sectors, up about 2%, followed by real estate, communication services and industrials, each up close to 1%. Energy and financials gained about 0.7%. Technology was the weakest sector, down about 0.8%, followed by health care, down about 0.6%, and consumer discretionary, slightly lower. The pattern showed investors trimming crowded AI holdings and moving into cyclical and value areas, while lower yields that day helped real estate.

This morning that pattern looks set to reverse, at least in part. With chip stocks bouncing and yields rising, technology is positioned to lead and rate-sensitive sectors such as real estate and utilities could lag.
Pre-market movers

items: Nvidia: up about 4%, recovering part of this week's losses despite reports it paused AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.
Chip and AI hardware stocks broadly: higher alongside Nvidia, following gains in Samsung and SK Hynix overnight.
Dell and Supermicro: in focus after reports said they told Southeast Asian buyers their Nvidia-based server orders cannot ship.
Gold and silver miners: in focus as gold rebounds about 2.7% and silver jumps more sharply.
Retailers such as Amazon, Walmart, Target and Best Buy: in focus on Black Friday traffic and online sales readings.

blocks.text: Oil

Brent crude is near $96.60 a barrel, roughly flat today, while U.S. crude (WTI) is up about 2.5% to near $85.80 as it catches up to Brent after Thursday's holiday-shortened trading. Prices jumped Wednesday after Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted drones there and did not confirm damage, while Reuters cited a person familiar with the matter saying the refinery was attacked. Attention now turns to Sunday's OPEC+ meeting, which is expected to address output policy for 2027; analysts are split on whether the group holds supply steady or adds barrels, with the IEA forecasting a global surplus.
Gold

Gold is up about 2.7% from Wednesday's settlement, near $3,630 to $3,660 an ounce depending on the contract and time, per CNBC data and other market reports. That is a rebound from Wednesday's 14-month low, when hot inflation data reinforced Fed-hike expectations. Silver has gained even more. Thin holiday volume has amplified the move. A near-certain Fed hike remains a headwind for gold, which pays no interest.
Crypto

Bitcoin is near $61,500, up about 1.3% from a day earlier, and Ether is near $1,735, up about 2%, per the app's market feed. Both remain far below their levels of a month ago and continue to track risk appetite in tech stocks and expectations for higher interest rates.
It is a light day for U.S. data. Both releases come at 8:30 a.m. ET and are rarely market-moving:

items: Advance goods trade balance for October: economists expect a deficit of about $135.9 billion, slightly wider than September's $134.9 billion. A wider gap would subtract from fourth-quarter GDP estimates.
Preliminary wholesale inventories for October: expected up 0.5% after 0.6% in September.
Market hours: stocks close at 1 p.m. ET; bonds at 2 p.m. ET.

blocks.text: No S&P 500 companies are scheduled to report today, which is typical for the day after Thanksgiving. The app's earnings calendar lists only a handful of small and foreign-listed companies. Retail sales readings from Black Friday will serve as the main corporate signal.

rows: Holiday-shortened session with no major earnings
Black Friday traffic and Adobe's online sales tally versus the 9.2% growth forecast
Any comment on the Southeast Asia shipment pause and export license timing

blocks.text: The weekend brings two events with market implications: Taiwan holds local elections on Saturday, and OPEC+ ministers meet Sunday to set 2027 output policy, which could move oil prices at Monday's open. Monday is also the last trading day of November, when month-end portfolio rebalancing can drive large moves. The U.S. data calendar then picks up: the ISM manufacturing index and JOLTS job openings on Tuesday, ADP private payrolls on Wednesday, the ISM services index on Thursday, and the November jobs report on Friday, December 4. That jobs report is the last major reading before the Fed's December 8 to 9 meeting, and with Fed officials in their quiet period, the data will be the main guide for rate expectations.

bottom_line: The morning tone is risk-on: AI stocks, global equities and gold are rebounding after a volatile week, while rising yields and a near-certain December Fed hike remain the main counterweight. Light holiday volume means today's moves may be a weak signal for next week.
